title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
Visual analytics focus This submission investigates where motor insurance profitability weakens, where volatility concentrates, and which segments deserve underwriting attention.



Transactions354,140Policy-year records from 2022 to 2024.


PremiumEUR 105,079,669Total premium across the analysed portfolio.


Loss ratio70.3%Overall profitable, but uneven across segments.




Insurers often know that a portfolio is underperforming before they understand why. This exercise uses a real motor insurance portfolio to show how visual analytics can move beyond dashboard reporting: the analysis combines distributional graphics, segment views and statistical validation to identify the portfolio segments most associated with weaker profitability and higher volatility.
The dataset was published on Mendeley Data as A detailed dataset of motor insurance policies with coverage-specific financial information. It contains anonymised motor insurance transactions from a Spanish non-life insurer between 2022 and 2024.



This report is organised around four questions.

What is the shape of the portfolio across policy, driver, vehicle and geographic characteristics?
How are premium, claim count, incurred loss and loss ratio distributed?
Which segments are associated with weaker profitability, measured mainly by loss ratio?
Which segments and coverages contribute most to claim frequency and volatility?

The analysis defines profitability as total_incurred / total_premium. Lower loss ratios are preferable because a smaller share of premium is absorbed by claims. Volatility is examined through claim concentration, loss-ratio dispersion and tail contribution.

text:
4.2 Policy Mix


Code
policy_type_summary |>
  mutate(policy_type_label = fct_reorder(policy_type_label, premium_share)) |>
  ggplot(aes(premium_share, policy_type_label, fill = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt_pct(premium_share)), hjust = -0.12, size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 0.55)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = insurance_palette["pine"],
    mid = insurance_palette["gold"],
    high = insurance_palette["brick"],
    midpoint = portfolio_kpi$loss_ratio,
    labels = percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium share by policy type",
    subtitle = "Fill colour shows segment loss ratio relative to the portfolio average.",
    x = "Share of total premium",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Loss ratio"
  )





Combined cover contributes the largest share of premium, while comprehensive covers carry greater claim intensity.




The portfolio is concentrated in combined cover and comprehensive-with-excess policies. Comprehensive-no-excess is smaller by volume but materially more loss-making, which makes it important despite its lower premium share.

text:
5.1 Premium and Incurred Loss


Code
p_premium <- policy_data |>
  filter(total_premium > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = insurance_palette["teal"], color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(prefix = "EUR ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium distribution",
    subtitle = "Log scale reveals the dense body and high-premium tail.",
    x = "Total premium, log scale",
    y = "Policies"
  )

p_incurred <- policy_data |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(total_incurred)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = insurance_palette["brick"], color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(prefix = "EUR ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Positive incurred loss distribution",
    subtitle = "Only policies with positive incurred cost are shown.",
    x = "Total incurred, log scale",
    y = "Policies"
  )

p_premium + p_incurred





Premium and incurred loss are right-skewed; most transactions have no incurred loss.




Premium is skewed, but incurred loss is far more concentrated. 88.1% of transactions have zero incurred loss, while 9.0% have losses exceeding premium. This asymmetry is the core reason why mean portfolio performance needs to be supplemented by tail and volatility views.

Code
policy_data |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio)) |>
  mutate(loss_ratio_capped = pmin(loss_ratio, 5)) |>
  ggplot(aes(loss_ratio_capped)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 70, fill = insurance_palette["pine"], color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = insurance_palette["brick"], linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, breaks = seq(0, 5, by = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Policy-level loss ratio, capped at 500% for readability",
    subtitle = "The dashed line marks the break-even threshold where claims equal premium.",
    x = "Loss ratio",
    y = "Policies"
  )





The loss-ratio distribution is zero-inflated with a long adverse tail.




The chart is intentionally capped at 500% to preserve readability. The uncapped 99th percentile is 1 236.4%, showing that a small number of policy transactions can dominate volatility.

text:
5.3 Claim Tail Concentration


Code
tail_markers <- tibble(policy_share = c(.01, .05, .10)) |>
  mutate(
    incurred_share = map_dbl(
      policy_share,
      \(threshold) tail_curve |>
        filter(policy_share <= threshold) |>
        summarise(max(incurred_share)) |>
        pull()
    )
  )

tail_curve |>
  ggplot(aes(policy_share, incurred_share)) +
  geom_line(color = insurance_palette["brick"], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = tail_markers, size = 2.7, color = insurance_palette["pine"]) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = tail_markers,
    aes(label = paste0(fmt_pct(policy_share), " policies: ", fmt_pct(incurred_share), " incurred")),
    min.segment.length = 0,
    seed = 608,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative incurred cost by largest-loss policies",
    subtitle = "Policies are sorted from highest to lowest incurred loss.",
    x = "Share of policies",
    y = "Share of total incurred"
  )





The top 1% of policies by incurred loss accounts for nearly half of incurred cost.




The top 1% of policy transactions by incurred loss contributes 49.7% of all incurred costs. This concentration indicates that volatility management should focus on tail-prone segments, not only average claim rates.

6.2 Policy Type and Profitability


Code
policy_type_summary |>
  mutate(policy_type_label = fct_reorder(policy_type_label, loss_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(loss_ratio, policy_type_label, fill = claim_frequency)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = portfolio_kpi$loss_ratio, linetype = "dashed", color = "#394642") +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt_pct(loss_ratio)), hjust = -0.08, size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1.05)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = insurance_palette["moss"], high = insurance_palette["brick"]) +
  labs(
    title = "Loss ratio by policy type",
    subtitle = "Dashed line marks the overall portfolio loss ratio.",
    x = "Loss ratio",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Claim frequency"
  )





Comprehensive-no-excess has the weakest loss ratio and highest claim frequency.




Comprehensive-no-excess has the highest loss ratio and claim frequency. This is consistent with product design: when the policyholder has no excess, smaller losses are more likely to be claimed, and the insurer absorbs more of the claim cost.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
6.3 Loss Ratio Dispersion


Code
loss_sample |>
  mutate(
    loss_ratio_capped = pmin(loss_ratio, 3),
    policy_type_label = fct_reorder(policy_type_label, loss_ratio_capped, .fun = median)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(loss_ratio_capped, policy_type_label, fill = policy_type_label)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.78, adjust = 0.7, point_interval = median_qi, .width = c(.5, .8)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rep(insurance_palette, length.out = nlevels(loss_sample$policy_type_label))) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampled loss-ratio distributions by policy type",
    subtitle = "Loss ratios are capped at 300% for display; summary tests use the full uncapped data.",
    x = "Loss ratio",
    y = NULL
  )





Policy types differ not only in average loss ratio, but also in dispersion.




The policy-type signal is statistically validated by a Kruskal-Wallis test of loss-ratio distributions: H = r round(unname(kruskal_policy$statistic), 1), p < 2.2e-16. A Fligner-Killeen variance test on log1p(loss_ratio) also rejects equal variance across policy types: chi-square = r round(unname(fligner_policy$statistic), 1), p < 2.2e-16. In short, policy type affects both profitability and volatility.

6.4 Coverage-Specific View


Code
coverage_summary_tbl |>
  mutate(coverage = fct_reorder(coverage, loss_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(loss_ratio, coverage)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = loss_ratio, y = coverage, yend = coverage), color = "#c4ccc8", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(size = premium_share, color = avg_severity), alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt_pct(loss_ratio)), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, .86)) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = percent, range = c(3, 10)) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = insurance_palette["teal"], high = insurance_palette["brick"], labels = label_dollar(prefix = "EUR ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Coverage-level loss ratio",
    subtitle = "Point size shows premium share; colour shows average claim severity.",
    x = "Loss ratio",
    y = NULL,
    size = "Premium share",
    color = "Avg severity"
  )





Liability and property damage dominate both premium and incurred loss.




Liability and property damage are the main profitability levers because they account for the majority of premium and incurred loss. Occupants has high average severity but very few claims, so it is more of a tail monitoring issue than a portfolio-wide profitability driver.

text:
6.5 Customer and Payment Signals


Code
segment_tbl <- bind_rows(
  bonus_summary |> transmute(segment = as.character(bonus_score_label), group = "Claims history", loss_ratio, claim_rate, premium_share),
  payment_summary |> transmute(segment = as.character(payment_frequency_label), group = "Payment frequency", loss_ratio, claim_rate, premium_share),
  business_summary |> transmute(segment = as.character(business_type_label), group = "Business origin", loss_ratio, claim_rate, premium_share),
  area_summary |> transmute(segment = as.character(circulation_area_label), group = "Circulation area", loss_ratio, claim_rate, premium_share)
)

segment_tbl |>
  mutate(segment = fct_reorder(segment, loss_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(loss_ratio, segment, color = claim_rate, size = premium_share)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = portfolio_kpi$loss_ratio, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7c8581") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = insurance_palette["pine"], high = insurance_palette["brick"], labels = percent) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = percent, range = c(2, 9)) +
  labs(
    title = "Bivariate segment scan",
    subtitle = "The strongest adverse signals are not limited to one variable family.",
    x = "Loss ratio",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Claim rate",
    size = "Premium share"
  )





Claims history, payment frequency and renewal status all show visible profitability differences.




Semiannual and quarterly payment policies show higher loss ratios than annual policies. Portfolio business also has a weaker loss ratio than new business. These patterns should not be read causally on their own, but they are useful segmentation clues for underwriting review.

  geom_hline(yintercept = portfolio_kpi$loss_ratio, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7c8581") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = portfolio_kpi$claim_frequency, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7c8581") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = segment), seed = 608, size = 3.1, max.overlaps = 30) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(accuracy = .01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = percent, range = c(2, 10)) +

Vehicle age and fuel type help explain claim frequency and profitability differences.




Younger drivers have high claim rates, but they are a small premium segment. Diesel vehicles show weaker profitability than gasoline vehicles, and urban circulation has higher claim frequency than rural circulation. These signals are useful for prioritising pricing refinements only after controlling for policy type and exposure.

text:
7.1 Frequency Model
To validate claim frequency drivers, a quasi-Poisson model was fitted with total_claims as the response and log(total_exposure) as an offset. Exponentiated coefficients are interpreted as claim frequency ratios relative to the reference category, holding other included variables constant.


Code
freq_plot <- frequency_effects |>
  mutate(effect_strength = abs(log(estimate))) |>
  slice_max(effect_strength, n = 18) |>
  mutate(effect = fct_reorder(effect, estimate))

freq_plot |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, effect, color = direction)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7c8581") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), height = .16, linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Higher frequency" = insurance_palette["brick"], "Lower frequency" = insurance_palette["pine"])) +
  labs(
    title = "Claim frequency ratios from quasi-Poisson model",
    subtitle = "Ratios above 1 indicate higher expected claim frequency than the reference level.",
    x = "Frequency ratio, log scale",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  )





The model confirms that policy type, claims history and payment frequency remain strong claim frequency signals after controls.




The largest modelled effects are associated with comprehensive covers. Comprehensive-no-excess policies have a much higher expected claim frequency than third-party-only policies, even after controlling for year, claims history, business origin, driver age, vehicle age, geography, payment frequency and fuel type.

text:
8.1 Main Findings
The portfolio is profitable overall, but the average masks clear pockets of pressure. Loss ratio deteriorated in 2024, comprehensive-no-excess policies show the weakest profitability, and incurred loss is highly concentrated in a small tail of transactions. Liability and property damage are the biggest portfolio-level levers because they carry both high premium share and high loss ratio.
Claims history, payment frequency, business origin, vehicle/fuel characteristics and circulation area are useful secondary signals. They are not all causal, but together they help identify segments where pricing, underwriting rules or claims management should be reviewed.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
8.2 Recommended Actions

Review comprehensive-no-excess pricing and deductible design because it has both high claim frequency and high loss ratio.
Monitor 2024 deterioration by separating exposure growth from severity inflation, especially in liability and property damage.
Build a tail-risk monitoring view for large losses, because the top 1% of policies by incurred cost contributes almost half of total incurred loss.
Use payment frequency and portfolio/new-business differences as underwriting diagnostics, then validate whether these are proxies for tenure, selection or customer risk.
Treat vehicle and geography signals as candidate rating refinements, especially diesel, urban circulation and higher-value vehicle segments.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
8.3 Limitations
The dataset is anonymised and does not include some common rating factors such as exact geography, claim dates, inflation indices, driving usage, no-claims discount details or external socioeconomic variables. The visual and statistical findings should therefore be interpreted as portfolio diagnostics rather than final pricing indications. A production actuarial model would require additional exposure validation, claim development checks and out-of-sample testing.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Contents


1BaselinePortfolio scale, premium, incurred loss and overall loss ratio.


2DistributionPremium shape, incurred loss skew and the policy-level loss tail.


3DriversPolicy type, coverage, claims history and payment frequency.


4ValidationDistribution tests and a claim frequency model with exposure offset.


5ActionsPractical underwriting and monitoring implications.



The deck moves from the whole portfolio into progressively sharper segment views. I first establish the baseline, then show the skewed distribution of losses, then move into policy type, coverage and customer signals. The final slides translate the evidence into actions.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Portfolio Baseline


Policy transactions354,140185,678 insured IDs across 2022-2024.


Exposure years250,325.9Exposure-weighted comparisons are used for frequency.


Total premiumEUR 105,079,669Portfolio scale before incurred loss.


Total incurredEUR 73,864,811Paid and reserved claim cost.


Loss ratio70.3%Profitable overall, but uneven by segment.


Underwriting profitEUR 31,214,859The headline hides a concentrated claims tail.



The portfolio contains 354,140 policy transactions and about 250,326 exposure years. The overall loss ratio is about 70.3%, which means the portfolio is profitable in aggregate. The important point is that aggregate profitability is not evenly distributed; we need segment and tail views to identify where underperformance and volatility are coming from.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Policy Mix


Combined cover is the largest premium block, followed by comprehensive-with-excess. Comprehensive-no-excess is smaller, but its colour already signals a weaker loss ratio. This tells us that a segment does not need to be the largest by premium to matter for portfolio quality.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Loss Distribution

88.1% of transactions have zero incurred loss, while 9.0% exceed break-even.

The portfolio is zero-inflated and right-skewed. Most transactions have no incurred loss, but the policies that do claim can produce a very wide range of costs. This is why mean loss ratio alone is not enough; volatility and tail concentration are central to the story.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
2024 Deterioration


Loss ratio was stable around the mid-60% range in 2022 and 2023, then moved to about 74.7% in 2024. This does not necessarily mean one root cause; it tells us that year should be treated as an important context variable when interpreting the segment results.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Policy Type Drives Profitability


Comprehensive-no-excess has the highest loss ratio and the highest claim frequency. This makes intuitive business sense because no-excess policies expose the insurer to more small and medium claims. It is the clearest product-level candidate for pricing or deductible review.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Volatility Differs by Policy Type

Kruskal-Wallis and Fligner-Killeen tests both return p < 2.2e-16.

The difference is not just in average loss ratio. The distributions also differ in dispersion, which matters for volatility. Both tests strongly reject equality across policy types: the Kruskal-Wallis test validates distributional differences, while the Fligner-Killeen test validates variance differences.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Coverage View


Liability and property damage have the highest strategic importance because they combine large premium shares with high loss ratios. Occupants coverage has high average severity, but few claims, so it is more of a tail-monitoring issue than a broad profitability driver.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Customer Signals


Poor and neutral claims-history groups show weaker results than good claims-history policies. Semiannual and quarterly payment frequencies are also less favourable than annual payment. These variables may be proxies for customer mix or tenure, so they should be treated as diagnostic flags before being used directly as pricing actions.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Frequency Model


The model confirms that policy type remains the strongest signal after controlling for year, claims history, business origin, driver age, vehicle age, geography, payment frequency and fuel type. Comprehensive-no-excess is far above the third-party-only reference level, which supports the visual findings.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Tail Concentration


The top 1% of policy transactions by incurred loss accounts for about half of total incurred cost. This is the volatility story in one chart: underwriting and claims teams should not only track averages, but also build monitoring around large-loss concentration.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
What To Do Next


1. DeductiblesReview comprehensive-no-excess pricing and deductible design.


2. 2024 DrilldownSeparate exposure growth from severity pressure in liability and property damage.


3. Tail WatchMonitor large-loss concentration instead of relying only on averages.


4. SelectionValidate payment and business-origin effects with tenure data.


5. Rating ReviewTest vehicle, fuel and circulation signals as candidate rating refinements.



The recommendations separate immediate portfolio review from longer-term modelling. The most direct action is the comprehensive-no-excess review. The second is to understand 2024 deterioration. The third is tail monitoring. The remaining actions should be explored with more data because they may represent customer selection effects rather than direct causes.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Limitations

Interpret as portfolio diagnostics, not final pricing indications. The dataset does not include exact geography, claim dates, inflation indices, driving usage, policy tenure, detailed no-claims discount history or external socioeconomic data.


The analysis is intentionally transparent and reproducible, but it is still constrained by the available variables. A production actuarial workflow would need exposure validation, claim development checks, external enrichment and out-of-sample testing before turning these insights into rating changes.

import json

Question 1 - What events and relationships led to the inappropriate release?
The crisis did not start at 17:25. Conclusion
The merger did not leak because the system randomly broke. It leaked because the organization had already normalized porous personal channels, advisory-only oversight, and improvisation under pressure. When the market narrative turned hostile, Legal and Social treated compliance as a moving boundary rather than a hard stop. The embargo was therefore not defeated by one rogue post; it was defeated by a system that had already learned how to route around its own guardrails.
